1. A rigorous RCT conducted only at a single urban tertiary hospital shows that a treatment works, with excellent internal validity. A district health officer wants to apply the finding in rural PHCs. What should she consider first, and what kind of evidence would answer it?

External validity: whether the effect is the same in rural PHC patients. That depends on whether the effect is modified by the ways PHC patients differ (severity, baseline nutrition, co-morbidity, adherence, follow-up care). The best evidence is consistency: trials or well-conducted observational studies in similar settings, or subgroup results from the original trial (tested for interaction) for patients like hers. Internal validity was the precondition, and it is met.

2. Explain why internal and external validity can pull against each other in study design.

Choices that strengthen internal validity (narrow eligibility, standardised protocols, intensive monitoring, excluding people likely to drop out) make the participants and conditions less like routine practice. The effect is then estimated cleanly but for a narrower population, so its transfer to others rests more on judgement.

3. Study A (n = 120) reports RR 1.9 (95% CI 0.9 to 4.0). Study B (n = 12,000), using the same exposure questionnaire with the same systematic error, reports RR 1.35 (95% CI 1.25 to 1.46). Which alternative explanation has Study B’s size dealt with, and which has it not?

Chance: B’s interval is narrow and excludes 1, so random variation is an unlikely explanation for its association. Size does nothing for bias or confounding: the same measurement error is present in B, and the narrow interval is now centred on an estimate that is still biased by it. (Confounding, too, is unchanged by n.)

1. A cohort has 100 exposed people (30 develop the outcome) and 100 unexposed (10 develop it), so the true RR is 3.0. Exposure is recorded with Se = 0.90 and Sp = 0.80, equally in people with and without the outcome. Compute the recorded 2 × 2 table and the recorded RR. What kind of misclassification is this, and in which direction did it move the estimate?

  1. Among the 40 with the outcome (30 exposed, 10 unexposed): recorded exposed = 0.90 × 30 + 0.20 × 10 = 27 + 2 = 29; recorded unexposed = 11.
  2. Among the 160 without (70 exposed, 90 unexposed): recorded exposed = 0.90 × 70 + 0.20 × 90 = 63 + 18 = 81; recorded unexposed = 79.
  3. Recorded exposed group: 29 + 81 = 110, risk 29 ÷ 110 = 0.264. Recorded unexposed: 11 + 79 = 90, risk 11 ÷ 90 = 0.122.
  4. Recorded RR = 0.264 ÷ 0.122 = 2.16, against a true 3.0.

Non-differential misclassification of a binary exposure (the same Se and Sp whatever the outcome). It moved the RR towards the null, as expected when Se + Sp > 1 (here 1.70).

2. In a case-control study of low birthweight, (a) interviewers who know which mothers had a low-birthweight baby ask them more follow-up questions about tobacco chewing, and (b) mothers of low-birthweight babies, looking for a reason, report chewing more completely. Name each bias and give one way to prevent each.

  1. Interviewer bias (information bias arising from the data collector): prevent with a scripted questionnaire asked identically of all, training, and interviewers kept unaware of case status where possible. (b) Recall bias (information bias arising from the participant’s memory): prevent by using exposure recorded before the outcome (antenatal cards), or by choosing controls with another adverse outcome that would prompt similar reflection. Both are differential misclassification, so the direction cannot be assumed.

3. Women taking an oral contraceptive visit a doctor more often than other women, and more hypertension is recorded among them. Is this observer bias or detection bias? How would you design the study to prevent it?

Detection bias: the exposure brings women under medical attention, so their blood pressure is measured more often and hypertension is found more often, whatever its true frequency. Observer bias would be a measurer reading blood pressure differently because she knows who takes the pill. Prevention: measure blood pressure in every participant on the same schedule with the same method (equal surveillance), ideally by staff blinded to contraceptive use.

1. Name the bias in each: (a) a study of coal miners finds their all-cause mortality lower than the state’s; (b) a case-control study of tuberculosis and diabetes recruits cases from patients currently on treatment at a DOTS centre; (c) a free cancer screening camp finds that participants have lower cancer mortality than the district; (d) women in a diet study eat more vegetables in the weeks they know they are being observed.

  1. Healthy-worker effect: miners were fit enough to be hired and to stay employed; compare exposed with less-exposed miners instead. (b) Neyman (prevalence–incidence) bias: prevalent cases on treatment exclude those who died early; if diabetes raises early TB mortality, diabetic cases are under-represented and the association is understated. Use newly diagnosed (incident) cases. (c) Volunteer (self-selection) bias: people who attend screening camps are often healthier and more health-conscious; a randomised comparison of invited and not-invited populations is needed. (Lead-time and length-time bias also threaten survival comparisons here.) (d) Hawthorne effect.

2. An oral cancer screening programme detects a cancer at age 52 that would have caused symptoms at 55; the patient dies at 58. Compute survival from diagnosis with and without screening and the lead time. What outcome measure should the programme’s evaluation use?

  1. With screening: 58 − 52 = 6 years.
  2. Without screening: 58 − 55 = 3 years.
  3. Lead time = 55 − 52 = 3 years, the whole apparent gain; age at death is 58 either way.

Evaluate by oral-cancer mortality (deaths per 100,000 per year) in populations randomised to screening or not, not by survival from diagnosis.

3. Which of Hill’s viewpoints is logically necessary for any causal claim, and why would a lack of specificity be a weak argument against tobacco as a cause of lung cancer?

Temporality: a cause must come before its effect; the other eight add weight but none is required. Specificity (one cause, one effect) is weak because many exposures cause several diseases: tobacco causes lung cancer, oral cancer, heart disease and more. Hill himself warned: “We must not, however, over-emphasise the importance of the characteristic.”

1. Two studies each find no association between a workplace exposure and a health outcome. Study X sampled workers well but did not measure smoking, a known confounder. Study Y measured everything but recruited from a clinic that sees mainly workers who fell ill. Explain why these problems differ, how each could be addressed, and how each could have hidden a real effect.

Study X has unmeasured confounding. Smoking was never recorded, so it cannot be adjusted for in these data. It can be addressed with new data (measure smoking, or a validation sub-sample), or bounded with a sensitivity analysis (§17.3.1): how strongly would smoking have to be related to exposure and outcome to change the conclusion? It could hide an effect if the confounding is negative: for example, if exposed workers smoke less than unexposed ones, and smoking raises the outcome risk, the harm of the exposure is offset.

Study Y has selection bias only if entry to the clinic depends on both exposure and outcome. Recruiting only workers who fell ill means everyone has, or is likely to have, the outcome; if exposed workers attend the clinic for exposure-related reasons as well, clinic attendance is a collider (§17.2.1) and the association among attenders can be pushed towards, or across, the null. No analysis of these data restores the missing workers; the fix is redesign (a cohort of all workers, or population-based cases and controls). Separately, a non-representative sample that did not depend on both would limit generalisability without biasing the association.

Both studies could also be affected by non-differential misclassification of exposure, which tends to push a real effect towards the null. “No association” is not “no effect” until these explanations are addressed.

2. An adjusted RR is 1.8 (95% CI 1.2 to 2.7). Compute the E-values for the estimate and the confidence limit. Would a confounder with RR_EU = RR_UD = 2 explain the association away? (For a protective RR of 0.5, what is the E-value?)

  1. Estimate: 1.8 + √(1.8 × 0.8) = 1.8 + √1.44 = 1.8 + 1.2 = 3.0.
  2. Lower limit (closer to the null): 1.2 + √(1.2 × 0.2) = 1.2 + √0.24 = 1.2 + 0.49 = 1.69.
  3. Confounder (2, 2): B = 4 ÷ 3 = 1.33. Corrected RR ≥ 1.8 ÷ 1.33 = 1.35, corrected lower limit ≥ 1.2 ÷ 1.33 = 0.90. It cannot explain away the point estimate (2 < 3.0) but could explain away the lower limit (2 > 1.69): the interval could then include 1.
  4. Protective RR 0.5: invert to 2.0; E-value = 2 + √(2 × 1) = 2 + 1.41 = 3.41.

3. A cohort adjusts for maternal education recorded only as “literate / not literate”, and an association remains. A colleague calls what remains “unmeasured confounding”. Correct her. Then name the three design-stage methods of controlling confounding and one limitation of each.

Education was measured, but coarsely. What remains is residual confounding: differences in education within each of the two categories still confound. Recording years of schooling or finer categories would reduce it. Unmeasured confounding refers to a confounder never recorded.

Design-stage methods: (1) Randomisation: balances measured and unmeasured confounders on average, but only when the exposure can ethically and practically be assigned. (2) Restriction: admit one level of the confounder only; it cannot confound, but numbers fall and the result applies only to that level. (3) Matching: make comparison groups alike on the confounder; the analysis must account for the matching (in case-control studies matching alone does not remove confounding), and a matched variable’s own effect cannot then be studied.

1. Name the reporting guideline for each: (a) a cluster-randomised trial of weekly iron–folic acid in schools; (b) a case-control study of neonatal sepsis; (c) the accuracy of a digital haemoglobin meter against the laboratory; (d) a systematic review of yoga for hypertension; (e) FGDs with ASHAs on home visits; (f) a risk score predicting pre-eclampsia.

  1. CONSORT, with its extension for cluster trials. (b) STROBE. (c) STARD. (d) PRISMA. (e) COREQ (or SRQR). (f) TRIPOD+AI, which supersedes TRIPOD 2015 (§17.4).

2. Rewrite for a results section: “Not exclusively breastfed infants had significantly more diarrhoea (χ² = 23.37, p < 0.001).” Use the numbers of §10.6.4.

“Diarrhoea occurred in 33 of 80 infants (41.3%) who were not exclusively breastfed and 14 of 120 (11.7%) who were, a risk ratio of 3.54 (95% CI 2.02 to 6.17; χ² = 23.37, p < 0.001).” The effect and its interval come first; the test statistic and p-value follow, if given at all.

3. A district survey finds that only 35% of pregnant women took 100 IFA tablets. The team then interviews 15 women who did not, choosing them to include different ages, parities and blocks, and stops when new interviews add no new reasons. Name the mixed-methods design, the sampling approach and the stopping rule.

Explanatory sequential design (quantitative first, qualitative to explain it). Purposive sampling, with maximum variation across age, parity and block. Stopping at saturation, when new data yield no new codes or themes; 15 in-depth interviews lies within the 9–17 range at which empirical studies reached saturation for fairly homogeneous groups (Hennink & Kaiser, 2022).
